rows.description: A pupil hears snickers or tittering behind a back or across a room. It can signal gossip, cruelty, nerves or an unrelated joke, so assuming the worst is risky, but repeated targeting deserves reporting to a trusted adult.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: trust

rows.description: A child learns that a classmate crying may mean hurt, sadness, anger, embarrassment or relief, and cannot be sure which. Offering quiet company and asking are you okay works better than laughing or guessing.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: amusement, sadness, anger, embarrassment

rows.description: A schoolchild blinks back tears, turns away or goes to the bathroom to avoid crying in front of peers. It shows fear of embarrassment; a trusted adult can normalise tears and offer a private space to recover.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: sadness, fear, embarrassment, trust

rows.description: A pupil hears booing or cheering at a match or school event. Booing can be friendly rivalry or unkind jeering, and cheering can pressure a person; children learn to consider the target's feelings before joining in.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A schoolchild recognises that shouting can signal anger, fear or a wish to be heard. Staying calm, stepping back and getting a teacher or parent is safer than shouting back, and shouted threats should always be reported.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: anger, fear, calm, trust

rows.description: A schoolchild reads an adult's sigh or huff as tiredness, boredom or annoyance. It is ambiguous and may be relief; asking is everything is fine can prevent a child from assuming they are the cause.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: anger, relief, boredom, tiredness
related concepts: boredom

rows.description: A child hears a tut or a click of the tongue meaning disapproval in some places, or a sound of sympathy or a yes in others. Culture and tone change the meaning, so a listener should not jump to conclusions.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: empathy

rows.subtype: Hmm, uh and um as thinking sounds [Expressing]
rows.description: A schoolchild says hmm, uh or um while thinking or unsure. These fillers show the mind at work rather than lack of knowledge, and teachers who wait a few seconds get better answers than those who rush.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A schoolchild says ugh at a chore or a smelly item and aha at a discovery. Ugh signals disgust, boredom or mild annoyance; aha marks a sudden click of understanding that a teacher can celebrate.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: anger, disgust, boredom
related concepts: boredom

rows.description: A pupil hears a flat, monotone voice from a tired teacher or a shy friend. It can show boredom, low mood, calm or a personal speaking style, including some neurodivergent voices, so it should not be read as not caring.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: shyness, boredom, tiredness, calm
related concepts: boredom
